title: Emergent Quantum Geometric Phases in Holey Graphene
authors: Pablo Canteli, Yuriko Baba, Juan Salvador-Sánchez, Jorge Estrada-Álvarez, Ana Pérez-Rodríguez, Carlos Sánchez-Sánchez, Vito Clericò, Takashi Taniguchi, Kenji Watanabe, Francisco Domínguez-Adame, Rafael A Molina, Enrique Diez, Elena Díaz, Mario Amado
abstract: In graphene and other two-dimensional materials, periodic modulations of the electron density can significantly alter the energy spectrum and transport properties. Here, we report magnetotransport measurements in encapsulated monolayer graphene with ultra-high-quality patterned periodic antidot lattices that preserve the intrinsic electronic properties of the material. This lithographically defined platform enables controlled access to commensurability and superlattice phenomena at length scales otherwise difficult to achieve. By systematically tuning the lattice dimensions, we reveal a hierarchy of classical commensurability features arising from cyclotron orbits with comparable radii that follow multiple classical trajectories, resulting in broadened resistance peaks beyond the conventional single-orbit picture. Superimposed on these features, we observe pronounced Brown-Zak oscillations arising from the quantum commensurability between the magnetic flux quantum and the unit cell of the engineered Bravais lattices. We demonstrate that the intrinsic geometric phase of our system is directly measurable and show a precise matching of the magnetic field periodicity to the lithographic periodic patterning, where moiré-like electronic spectra can be geometrically generated in single-layer graphene without the need for twist, lattice mismatch, or multilayer stacking. Our results establish nanopatterned graphene as a clean, tunable, and scalable platform for realizing and exploring moiré physics through on-demand real-space design
summary: This work reports on magnetotransport measurements in graphene patterned with antidot lattices to study quantum geometric phases. The authors demonstrate that these engineered superlattices create moiré-like electronic structures in single-layer graphene. This establishes a clean, scalable platform for realizing and measuring fundamental quantum phenomena in 2D materials.
main_problem: The paper investigates the emergence and direct measurement of intrinsic quantum geometric phases in graphene by engineering periodic potentials.
main_result: The patterned antidot lattice successfully generates moiré-like electronic spectra in single-layer graphene without requiring twist or multilayer stacking, establishing a tunable platform for exploring moiré physics.
method: Magnetotransport measurements ($R_{xx}$ vs. magnetic field) are performed on lithographically patterned graphene samples.
model_or_system: The physical system is encapsulated monolayer graphene patterned with ultra-high-quality periodic antidot lattices. The analysis combines classical commensurability features (Weiss peaks) with quantum interference effects (Brown-Zak oscillations).
key_observables: Longitudinal magnetoresistance ($R_{xx}$), commensurability peaks ($H_k$), and Brown-Zak oscillations.
important_parameters: Antidot diameters ($\Theta$) ranging from 50 nm to 300 nm; carrier mobility ($\mu$) $\sim 10^5 	ext{ cm}^2/	ext{Vs}$.
main_assumptions: The intrinsic geometric phase is directly measurable and the patterned lattice acts as a clean, tunable superlattice potential.
figures_summary: Figures show device schematics, optical micrographs of the antidot lattice, and magnetoresistance ($R_{xx}$) measurements resolving distinct commensurability peaks ($H_k$).
paper_structure: The paper progresses from demonstrating the physical platform (patterned graphene) to measuring classical commensurability features, and finally observing quantum interference effects like Brown-Zak oscillations, confirming the geometric phase measurement.
why_interesting: The ability to engineer moiré physics in a single layer via lithography, rather than relying on complex stacking or twisting, provides a highly controllable platform for studying geometric phases relevant to topological physics and quantum transport.
